# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites

rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

# Working in this repo

The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
what follows is everything else.

**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
telling you about.

**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape at the time, not
about the rule — re-ask it after the tree changes.** `on-device-privacy`'s
"everything lives in one deletable directory" sat as prose because proving it
looked like it needed data-flow tracking of a `FileManager` write target back to
its declaration — true while the Python reference had many entry points, and
false the moment that tree went away: the native app has exactly two persistent
path roots, both the same search-path lookup, so constraining the *root*
constrains every path derived from it and no tracing is needed. A removal, a
migration, or a consolidation can collapse the entry points a rule has to cover,
so when a sweep meets prose a previous sweep left behind, re-derive the objection
against today's sources instead of trusting the recorded verdict.

**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out — hand
the sibling check a violating file before dropping a rule as a duplicate.** Three
sweeps in a row left `on-device-privacy`'s "the app listens on no socket" as
prose, each reasoning that an `NWListener` needs `import Network` and
`no-network-client` already bans that. True of that one API, false of the
capability: `socket(2)` comes free with `import Foundation` (Darwin is
re-exported), `NSXPCListener`/`CFSocket*`/`NSSocketPort` are Foundation types, and
an embedded HTTP server arrives as its own import — a file whose entire content
was `let fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)` passed `check_the_world`
untouched. A ban list only covers the routes whoever wrote it thought of, so the
routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it; running it
against a file that breaks the rule costs a minute and is the only step that can
disagree with you.

**Write a check as a positive whitelist over an enumerated API surface, not as a
list of the bad cases.** `single-storage-directory` flags any search-path lookup
whose directory argument is not the literal `.applicationSupportDirectory`,
rather than enumerating the directories we don't want. Matching the allowed case
buys two things a ban list can't: a `SearchPathDirectory` case that doesn't exist
yet is caught the day it lands, and a non-literal argument (`urls(for: dir, in:)`)
becomes a finding too — indirection is precisely what would otherwise defeat the
check, so refusing to reason about it is a feature. Only invert this where the
allowed set is genuinely open-ended.

---

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log — the `single-storage-directory` check holds this mechanically,
by allowing `.applicationSupportDirectory` and nothing else as a search-path root.
"Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a user *acts on* — someone who
deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them went with it. So a feature
needing somewhere new to keep things extends that directory rather than earning a
second one; the one path macOS dictates, not us, is a Login Item registration,
which names no directory of its own.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

---

# Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing)

Each pack states what it owns and what it does not. When a rule, doc, skill or check could live in more than one, this table decides it — and "no pack fits" means a new pack or the project's own `local_packs/`, never the baseline by default.

| Pack | Belongs | Does not belong |
|---|---|---|
| `barriers` | directed folder-access graph rules — which directories may never reference which, plus the exceptions each rule allows | where a file should live or naming conventions — that is basics file-placement, not an access barrier |
| `basics` | cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills | technology-specific content — its own tech pack; GitHub Actions workflow or platform behaviour — github-actions; git procedure — git-github |
| `git-github` | git and GitHub procedure: commit layering, branch and merge mechanics, squash-merge recovery, PR and merge-to-main commands | the issue-branch-PR lifecycle rules themselves — basics; workflow YAML and Actions runtime behaviour — github-actions |
| `github-actions` | workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls | git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack |
| `grow_with_claudinite` | rules and tasks for capturing lessons into local packs — extraction, dedup, conversation logs, skill-usage folding | repo housekeeping of issues, PRs and branches — that is tidy-repo; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `tidy-repo` | housekeeping of open issues, pull requests and branches in one repo — triage verdicts, standing trackers, assess-vs-act policy | extracting lessons into packs — that is grow_with_claudinite; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `laughcounter` (local) | LaughCounter's general working lessons about this repo, its build, its macOS packaging, and how its own local-pack checks are authored | the on-device privacy boundary — that is on-device-privacy |

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	# Growth — discover local packs (per repo)
2	
3	A weekly reflection on **this repo's own** captured knowledge: knowing the Claudinite packs already available to it, notice when project-specific knowledge is worth organizing into a **new local pack** — and author it. A local operation: it writes only the repo's **own** `.claudinite/local/packs/`, landing through a PR **a human reviews** (unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), which auto-merges; the shared canon stays human-gated too — lifting a local pack up is the central promote task's job). Finding nothing new worth a pack is a perfectly good, common outcome.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue. There is no windowed Context to bind — the opportunity is standing (knowledge that was never organized into a pack, not a recent change), so examine the repo as it is.
6	
7	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: it opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge**. Extract auto-merges because it adds prose or a rule to territory a local pack already owns; a **new pack** ships new `.mjs` conformance checks that run at every Stop and in CI the moment it merges — a check can break CI, so it's reviewed, exactly as the sibling [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md) is.
8	
9	## Conventions used in this doc
10	
11	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`) for issue/PR work; read the repo's own tree from the working checkout (local git), never a cross-repo clone.
12	- **The repo's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — the repo's own packs.
13	- **The available canon packs** are the read-only mounted shelf under `.claudinite/shared/packs/` — what Claudinite already homes for this repo. Knowing the shelf is how you avoid re-creating locally what the canon already covers.
14	
15	## The pipeline
16	
17	### 1. Manifest the repo's own stack
18	
19	Catalogue what this project is built on and how it ships — grounded in its files (dependency/build manifests, lockfiles, toolchain/config, CI and release workflows, packaging/signing scripts, source structure, docs), citing the concrete evidence. Do **not** yet consult the pack shelf or decide anything about packs — this step only observes.
20	
21	**Never infer from "projects like this usually…"; if the repo doesn't show it, it is not in the manifest.** If something is present but appears vestigial or aspirational (declared but unused), include it and say so. Be **comprehensive over concise**: a later step filters and decides, so a true item you omit is lost, while an over-included one is cheaply dropped. When unsure whether something rises to an entry, include it with the `?` flag.
22	
23	Catalogue across **three axes**. Put each item under the single axis that fits best; when it genuinely spans two, place it under the primary and cross-note the other.
24	
25	- **Technologies** — languages and their versions, runtimes, frameworks, build systems, and the major libraries that shape how you write and build here (the load-bearing ones, not every transitive dependency).
26	- **External services / APIs** the project integrates with.
27	- **Deployment / distribution mechanisms** — how it ships and to where.
28	
29	For **each** item report: **name**; **axis**; **evidence** (the file(s), and what they show); **what it is in this repo** (one line); **prominence** — one of `core` (the project is built on it), `supporting` (used but peripheral), `vestigial` (present but apparently unused); and a **`?` flag** if you are uncertain the item is real or correctly characterised. Prominence is a factual read of how central the item is *in this repo* — **not** a judgment about whether it deserves any downstream treatment. Output the manifest as Markdown grouped under the three axis headings, one bullet per item with the fields labelled.
30	
31	### 2. Find the gap — what is pack-worthy but unhomed
32	
33	Now hold the manifest against two things: the **available canon packs** (`.claudinite/shared/packs/`) and the repo's **existing local packs**. A candidate for a new **local** pack is a technology or domain that:
34	
35	- the repo genuinely uses (not `vestigial`), and carries real, reusable working knowledge for — a build/config gotcha, a domain rule, a project-specific procedure that recurs; **and**
36	- **no canon pack already homes** — a technology is **homed**, so drop it, when any pack owns it, **a stub pack included** (if the canon covers it, the repo should just *declare that canon pack*, not re-create it locally — note that as the action instead); **and**
37	- the repo's **existing local packs don't already capture** (if a local pack owns that territory, a new rule belongs in it — that's [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md)'s job, not a new pack).
38	
39	What remains is project-specific knowledge that deserves its own local pack: a domain the project works in, or a technology the canon doesn't home, with enough captured knowledge to justify a pack rather than a loose rule.
40	
41	### 3. Author the local pack — distilled from the repo's real usage
42	
43	For each candidate, author a populated pack under `.claudinite/local/packs/<name>/`, distilled from **how this project actually works** — never from imagination. Apply the [generate-project-instructions](../../skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) method (don't re-derive it): descend the promotion ladder ([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)) — a rule a deterministic check can carry becomes the **check plus a see-it-fail fixture** (fires on a violating input, quiet on a clean one), a procedure with a nameable trigger becomes a skill, and only signature-less judgment lands as `RULES.md` prose. Ground and cite every rule in the project's real files. **Never pad** with speculative best-practice rules the evidence doesn't demonstrate; a rule you can't ground, you don't write — a smaller honest pack beats a padded one. And **never open an empty stub to fill later**. Write the pack files (`RULES.md`, `pack.mjs`, `README.md`), register it, and **declare it** in the repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` so it actually activates.
44	
45	### 4. Open the PR for review
46	
47	Land the new pack (and its declaration) through a single PR on a per-run-unique branch (see [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)) — title `Claudinite growth: discover local pack <name>`, and **put the issue reference in the commit message**: `Refs #<n>` for this task's tracking issue (below), in the commit itself, not only the PR body, so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. **Never arm auto-merge** — the reviewer is the point. A new check must still ship green (see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one) so CI stays green and the reviewer has something mergeable; a rule that can't be made a confident check lands as prose instead.
48	
49	## Tracking
50	
51	The standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Discover Local Packs`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it** — its state carries no meaning, only the log does. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the pack authored (technology/domain + the rungs its rules landed on), or "nothing new worth a local pack this run", and any "should declare canon pack X instead" note. For a candidate you found nothing groundable for, name it and why.
52	
53	## What this task must never do
54	
55	- **Never touch the shared canon or another repo** — it writes only this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.
56	- **Never re-create locally what a canon pack already homes** — declare the canon pack instead, and note it.
57	- **Never author from imagination or pad, and never open an empty stub** — every rule traces to the project's real usage; a pack may be small, it may not be invented.
58	- **Never add a rule to a territory an existing local pack already owns** — that is growth-extract's job; this task is for *new* packs.
59	- **Never conflate steps 1 and 2** — the manifest step catalogues and never consults the pack shelf; the gap step is where the shelf and the pack decision come in.
60	- **Never arm auto-merge** — a new pack's checks reach every session and every CI run in this repo; the reviewer is what stands between a wrong check and a red repo.
61	- **Run on `opus`** — judging pack-worthiness and authoring a pack (checks and fixtures included) is heavy judgment; a reviewer is a backstop, not a substitute for getting it right. This task declares `agent_model: opus`.

=== laughcounter/RULES ===
# Working in this repo

The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
what follows is everything else.

**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
telling you about.

**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape at the time, not
about the rule — re-ask it after the tree changes.** `on-device-privacy`'s
"everything lives in one deletable directory" sat as prose because proving it
looked like it needed data-flow tracking of a `FileManager` write target back to
its declaration — true while the Python reference had many entry points, and
false the moment that tree went away: the native app has exactly two persistent
path roots, both the same search-path lookup, so constraining the *root*
constrains every path derived from it and no tracing is needed. A removal, a
migration, or a consolidation can collapse the entry points a rule has to cover,
so when a sweep meets prose a previous sweep left behind, re-derive the objection
against today's sources instead of trusting the recorded verdict.

**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out — hand
the sibling check a violating file before dropping a rule as a duplicate.** Three
sweeps in a row left `on-device-privacy`'s "the app listens on no socket" as
prose, each reasoning that an `NWListener` needs `import Network` and
`no-network-client` already bans that. True of that one API, false of the
capability: `socket(2)` comes free with `import Foundation` (Darwin is
re-exported), `NSXPCListener`/`CFSocket*`/`NSSocketPort` are Foundation types, and
an embedded HTTP server arrives as its own import — a file whose entire content
was `let fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)` passed `check_the_world`
untouched. A ban list only covers the routes whoever wrote it thought of, so the
routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it; running it
against a file that breaks the rule costs a minute and is the only step that can
disagree with you.

**Write a check as a positive whitelist over an enumerated API surface, not as a
list of the bad cases.** `single-storage-directory` flags any search-path lookup
whose directory argument is not the literal `.applicationSupportDirectory`,
rather than enumerating the directories we don't want. Matching the allowed case
buys two things a ban list can't: a `SearchPathDirectory` case that doesn't exist
yet is caught the day it lands, and a non-literal argument (`urls(for: dir, in:)`)
becomes a finding too — indirection is precisely what would otherwise defeat the
check, so refusing to reason about it is a feature. Only invert this where the
allowed set is genuinely open-ended.

=== on-device-privacy/README ===
# on-device-privacy

LaughCounter's defining constraint as a local pack: an always-on living-room microphone whose audio
never leaves the machine. Distilled from this repo's own sources and requirements
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, the README *Privacy* section,
`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/`) — the promise was stated in three docs and enforced nowhere.

Local pack, declared by hand as `local/on-device-privacy` (no fingerprint). It covers the native
app, which since the Python reference was removed is the only implementation.

| Rule | How enforced |
| --- | --- |
| No outbound client in capture path | `no-network-client` check (`mac/Sources/**.swift`) |
| Speech recognition on-device | `on-device-speech` check (`SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest`) |
| Metadata persists, audio doesn't | `no-audio-persistence` check (`AVAudioFile`/`AVAudioRecorder`/`ExtAudioFileCreateWithURL`/`AudioFileCreateWithURL`) |
| One deletable directory | `single-storage-directory` check (only `.applicationSupportDirectory` as a search-path root) |
| No server / listener | `no-listener` check (`NWListener`/`NSXPCListener`/`CFSocket*`/`SocketPort`/`socket(2)`/an embedded HTTP-server import) |
| No egress at all | `RULES.md` prose |
| Usage strings stay true | `RULES.md` prose |

Fixtures: `pack.test.mjs` — `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs`.
Each check has a violating fixture it fires on and the repo's real files it stays quiet on. They sit
in the pack, not alongside the app sources (`claudinite-isolation`).
=== RULES ===
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log — the `single-storage-directory` check holds this mechanically,
by allowing `.applicationSupportDirectory` and nothing else as a search-path root.
"Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a user *acts on* — someone who
deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them went with it. So a feature
needing somewhere new to keep things extends that directory rather than earning a
second one; the one path macOS dictates, not us, is a Login Item registration,
which names no directory of its own.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

# Build LaughCounter.app from the Swift package. Runs on macOS (locally or in CI).
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."   # -> mac/

echo "Building release binary…"
swift build -c release

APP="dist/LaughCounter.app"
rm -rf "$APP"
mkdir -p "$APP/Contents/MacOS" "$APP/Contents/Resources"

BIN="$(swift build -c release --show-bin-path)/LaughCounter"
cp "$BIN" "$APP/Contents/MacOS/LaughCounter"
cp "Resources/Info.plist" "$APP/Contents/Info.plist"

# App icon: build a multi-resolution AppIcon.icns from the 1024² master PNG.
# The master PNG is committed, so this step only needs macOS's sips + iconutil.
ICON_SRC="Resources/AppIcon.png"
if [ -f "$ICON_SRC" ] && command -v sips >/dev/null && command -v iconutil >/dev/null; then
    echo "Building app icon…"
    ICONSET="$(mktemp -d)/AppIcon.iconset"
    mkdir -p "$ICONSET"
    for pair in "16 16x16" "32 16x16@2x" "32 32x32" "64 32x32@2x" \
                "128 128x128" "256 128x128@2x" "256 256x256" "512 256x256@2x" \
                "512 512x512" "1024 512x512@2x"; do
        set -- $pair
        sips -z "$1" "$1" "$ICON_SRC" --out "$ICONSET/icon_$2.png" >/dev/null
    done
    iconutil -c icns "$ICONSET" -o "$APP/Contents/Resources/AppIcon.icns"
    rm -rf "$(dirname "$ICONSET")"
else
    echo "warning: AppIcon.png or sips/iconutil missing — app will use the default icon"
fi

# sign for real with the Hardened Runtime + entitlements so the .dmg can be
# notarized by Apple and opens with no Gatekeeper warning. CI sets this from a
# secret; see the DMG workflows and scripts/notarize-dmg.sh.
#
# Otherwise fall back to an ad-hoc signature — fine for personal use, but macOS
# will block the first launch. Get past it with System Settings → Privacy &
# Security → "Open Anyway", or: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>.
# See mac/README.md "Install".
if [ -n "${MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY:-}" ]; then
    echo "Signing with Developer ID (Hardened Runtime): $MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY"
    codesign --force --options runtime \
        --entitlements "Resources/LaughCounter.entitlements" \
        --sign "$MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY" "$APP"
    codesign --verify --strict --verbose=2 "$APP"
else
    echo "No MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY set — using ad-hoc signature (not notarizable)."
    codesign --force --deep --sign - "$APP" || echo "warning: ad-hoc codesign failed (continuing)"
fi

echo "Built $APP"

set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."   # -> mac/

DMG="dist/LaughCounter.dmg"
STAGE="dist/dmg-stage"

if [ ! -d "$APP" ]; then

fi

rm -rf "$STAGE" "$DMG"
mkdir -p "$STAGE"
cp -R "$APP" "$STAGE/"
ln -s /Applications "$STAGE/Applications"   # drag-to-Applications shortcut

name: Release macOS DMG

# Publishes the DMG to GitHub Releases so the README's stable "latest release"
# link (releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg) always resolves.
#
# It runs automatically on every push to `main` that touches the app: it builds
# the DMG and creates/updates the Release for the current app version (read from
# Info.plist), attaching LaughCounter.dmg. GITHUB_TOKEN can create the tag and
# Release from within Actions (a session's git proxy cannot). Publishing a Release
# from the GitHub UI, or a manual dispatch, work too.

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "mac/**"
      - ".github/workflows/release-macos-dmg.yml"
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write           # create the tag/Release and attach the .dmg

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: macos-14
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: mac
        shell: bash   # runs steps with `bash -o pipefail` so piped commands fail loudly
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Swift toolchain
        run: swift --version

      # Signing + notarization only run when the repo has the signing secrets
      # configured (same set as build-macos-dmg.yml). Without them the published
      # DMG is ad-hoc-signed and users clear Gatekeeper manually (mac/README.md).
      - name: Detect signing secrets
        id: signing
        env:
          MACOS_CERT_P12: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_P12 }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$MACOS_CERT_P12" ]; then
            echo "enabled=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "enabled=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "::notice::No MACOS_CERT_P12 secret set — publishing an ad-hoc (unnotarized) DMG."
          fi

      - name: Import Developer ID certificate
        if: steps.signing.outputs.enabled == 'true'
        env:
          MACOS_CERT_P12: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_P12 }}
          MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          KEYCHAIN="$RUNNER_TEMP/signing.keychain-db"
          KEYCHAIN_PW="$(uuidgen)"
          security create-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PW" "$KEYCHAIN"
          security set-keychain-settings -lut 21600 "$KEYCHAIN"
          security unlock-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PW" "$KEYCHAIN"
          echo "$MACOS_CERT_P12" | base64 --decode > "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12"
          security import "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12" -k "$KEYCHAIN" \
            -P "$MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD" -T /usr/bin/codesign
          security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple: -s -k "$KEYCHAIN_PW" "$KEYCHAIN" >/dev/null
          # Make our keychain searchable alongside the login keychain.
          security list-keychains -d user -s "$KEYCHAIN" \
            $(security list-keychains -d user | sed 's/["[:space:]]//g')
          rm -f "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12"

      - name: Build LaughCounter.app
        env:
          MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY: ${{ steps.signing.outputs.enabled == 'true' && secrets.MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY || '' }}
        run: bash scripts/build-app.sh

      - name: Package .dmg
        run: bash scripts/make-dmg.sh

      - name: Notarize .dmg
        if: steps.signing.outputs.enabled == 'true'
        env:
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_PASSWORD }}
        run: bash scripts/notarize-dmg.sh

      - name: Resolve release tag
        id: rel
        # On a UI-published release, use its tag; otherwise derive v<version> from
        # the app's Info.plist so a version bump publishes a new Release.
        run: |
          if [ "$GITHUB_EVENT_NAME" = "release" ]; then
            tag="$GITHUB_REF_NAME"
          else
            version="$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :CFBundleShortVersionString' Resources/Info.plist)"
            tag="v$version"
          fi
          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Publish Release with DMG
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        # Create the Release (and its tag at this commit) with the DMG attached; if
        # it already exists, just (re)upload the DMG. A Release made with
        # GITHUB_TOKEN does not re-fire the `release` event, so there's no loop.
        run: |
          tag='${{ steps.rel.outputs.tag }}'
          gh release create "$tag" dist/LaughCounter.dmg \
            --title "LaughCounter $tag" --generate-notes --target "$GITHUB_SHA" \
          || gh release upload "$tag" dist/LaughCounter.dmg --clobber

1	# macOS audio lifecycle — releasing the mic on every path
2	
3	Hard-won rules for `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` (AudioHub, AppDelegate's restart
4	machinery, VoiceCommand). Read before touching engine start/stop, sleep/wake, or
5	exit handling.
6	
7	**The invariant.** If this process ends — or intentionally stops capture — while
8	the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
9	device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
10	Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
11	*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
12	overlap restarts. (#22)
13	
14	## Never reuse an `AVAudioEngine` across a device change (#61)
15	
16	An `AVAudioEngine` caches the input hardware format when its input node is first
17	materialized, and **the cache does not follow the device**. After CoreAudio tears
18	the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod dropping its contexts
19	when the display sleeps — `inputNode.outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports the
20	*old* rate, while `installTap` validates against the freshly-queried hardware
21	format. They disagree, and `installTap` raises an **uncatchable** NSException:
22	`required condition is false: format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate`.
23	
24	This killed the app on **every** configuration change — six for six over fifteen
25	days on the owner's Mac mini, the longest outage fifteen days of nobody noticing.
26	The pre-tap guard added in #22 did not help, because it compared the stale cache
27	against itself and always passed: not the microsecond race its comment assumed,
28	but a design gap. So `AudioHub.prepareFormat()` **builds a new engine every time**
29	(stopping the old one first — dropping the last reference to a *running* engine
30	abandons its IOProc on the device, the wedge condition). Three consequences:
31	
32	- **The crash was also the mic-wedge cause.** An uncaught NSException aborts the
33	  process, so `applicationWillTerminate` never runs and the tap's IOProc is left
34	  registered — the BRIO went dead until physically re-plugged. The exit-path rule
35	  below calls crash teardown "residual risk"; at six crashes in fifteen days it
36	  was the main risk.
37	- **A replaced engine invalidates an observer bound to the old instance**, so
38	  `AudioHub` owns the `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` observation and
39	  republishes it via `onConfigurationChange` (delivered on main). Registering it
40	  from `AppDelegate` against `audio.engine` would go quiet after the first
41	  restart — and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
42	  its microphone vanished.
43	- **Swift cannot catch `NSException`**, so the last line of defence is a few
44	  lines of Objective-C (`Sources/ObjCExceptionTrap`, its own SwiftPM target — our
45	  source, not a dependency). Catching one is only safe because these calls
46	  validate *before* mutating anything; don't wrap framework calls in general.
47	  Treat the trap as **unproven** until something demonstrates it catching a real
48	  raise: the exception has to unwind through the intervening Swift closure frame,
49	  which is not guaranteed to work.
50	
51	**A new engine must have a node attached before `prepare()`.** `AVAudioEngine`
52	initializes its graph inside `prepare()` and asserts `inputNode != nullptr ||
53	outputNode != nullptr` — another uncatchable NSException. A freshly constructed
54	engine has neither: `inputNode` is created lazily *on first access*, and touching
55	the property is what attaches it. `AudioHub.makeEngine()` does that as part of
56	building one, so no call ordering elsewhere can get it wrong. The single-engine
57	code satisfied this by accident — `requestListening()`'s `stop()` reached
58	`engine.inputNode.removeTap(onBus: 0)` long before any `prepare()` — and
59	rebuilding the engine *after* that call removed the accident: v0.3.0 crashed one
60	second into every launch. (#72)
61	
62	**`outputFormat(forBus:)` cannot tell you the microphone is gone.** For the input
63	node, `inputFormat(forBus: 0)` is the *hardware* format — the one `installTap`
64	asserts on. `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` is the bus's output format, and with the
65	device torn down it still reports a plausible 48 kHz while `inputFormat` reports
66	0. Guards written against `outputFormat` therefore pass while the mic is absent
67	and leave `installTap` to raise: measured, once a minute for the whole 28 minutes
68	the displays slept. Validate `inputFormat`, and require it to agree with
69	`outputFormat`, before installing a tap. (#76)
70	
71	**The mic is unavailable for as long as the displays sleep** — on this Mac mini
72	with a Logitech BRIO, `pmset displaysleepnow` tears the input down within
73	~20 seconds and it does not return until the displays wake (28 minutes in one
74	measurement). Recovery arrives as an `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` when the
75	device reappears. So a *bounded* retry ladder is the wrong shape — it expires
76	with the cause fully present — and the give-up message must not blame the
77	hardware. Back off to a ceiling and keep checking; a cheap format read once a
78	minute is nowhere near the rate that cycles a mic.
79	
80	**Compile-green is not a gate for this file.** Two crash-on-launch builds shipped
81	past CI, which only runs `swift build`. Every raise-vs-throw bug here is invisible
82	to the compiler and reachable in the first second of a run, so a change to
83	`AudioHub` is not verified until it has actually started on a Mac.
84	
85	Reproduce it without waiting for hardware to misbehave: let the display sleep
86	(`displaysleep 20`), and coreaudiod tears its contexts down seconds later.
87	
88	## `listening` never meant audio was arriving — measure the buffers (#79)
89	
90	`listening` is set because `engine.start()` returned. It has never meant a single
91	buffer arrived, and the settle-time reconciliation checks `audio.isRunning`, which
92	a running-but-dead engine also satisfies. So the app could hold a wedged device
93	for an entire evening with the menu bar reporting "listening" — the one symptom
94	the owner sees, saying the one thing that isn't true. Every round of this bug was
95	therefore reconstructed after the fact from a log whose only claim was `listening
96	started`.
97	
98	`AudioDiagnostics` closes that: the tap reports every buffer, and 15s of silence
99	while we believe we are capturing is an `AUDIO STALL` line plus a distinct menu
100	state. Three things about it are load-bearing:
101	
102	- **Read the HAL, don't build an engine, when you only want to know whether a mic
103	  is there.** `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` is a property query that does *not*
104	  open the device, so sampling it every five seconds forever is free and cannot
105	  cycle anything. `AudioHub.prepareFormat()` is the opposite — it builds an
106	  engine, materializes `inputNode` (which opens the device) and calls `prepare()`
107	  *before* validating — so the "cheap format read" the retry-ladder comment in
108	  `AppDelegate` claims is actually a full device open/close, once a minute for as
109	  long as the mic is missing.
110	- **`kAudioDevicePropertyDeviceIsRunningSomewhere` is the wedge oracle.** It is
111	  true when *any* process has IO running on the device. No buffers arriving while
112	  it is true means the running stream is ours and it is dead — as opposed to the
113	  device having gone away, which looks identical from inside the app.
114	- **Measure buffer silence with `systemUptime`, not `Date()`** — the exact
115	  opposite of the sleep-duration rule above, for the opposite reason: this is
116	  "how long has the stream been silent *while we were awake*", so a sleep in the
117	  middle must not be counted as silence.
118	
119	Log on state change, not on a timer: a heartbeat every ten minutes, and an
120	immediate line when a stall starts or ends or the device set changes. (Same
121	reason `scheduleStartRetry` announces its slow mode once — a line a minute for
122	half an hour buries everything else.)
123	
124	## Opening the default input creates an aggregate device — so a restart churns two
125	
126	The first field output from `AudioDiagnostics` showed the input device set is not
127	just the microphone:
128	
129	```
130	inputs=[*"Logitech BRIO"/usb/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y/running=n
131	        "CADefaultDeviceAggregate-70999-0"/grup/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y/running=n]
132	```
133	
134	That second entry is a **private aggregate device** (`grup` =
135	`kAudioDeviceTransportTypeAggregate`) that coreaudiod creates *per client* when
136	an app captures from the default input, so the client can survive the default
137	changing under it. It was already present in the first sample, before capture
138	started — i.e. **merely constructing `AudioHub` creates it**, because
139	`makeEngine()` materializes `inputNode`, and touching that property opens the
140	default input device.
141	
142	The consequence is that the retry ladder's cost was under-estimated twice over.
143	`prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` does not merely open and close the
144	microphone; it tears down and recreates an aggregate device inside coreaudiod on
145	every attempt — a much heavier operation than a device open, and one that has to
146	re-resolve the default input each time. That is what runs once a minute, for as
147	long as the mic is missing.
148	
149	It also means the *device set itself* changes on every one of those cycles, as
150	the aggregate comes and goes. So a diagnostic that alarms on "the device list
151	changed" alarms on our own restarts. Separate the two: an appearing/vanishing
152	device (or a changed rate, channel count or alive flag) is a hardware event;
153	`isRunningSomewhere` flipping is usually just us. `AudioDiagnostics.identities()`
154	is that split.
155	
156	## What the first day of field data settled — and what it did **not** (#79)
157	
158	Written down because the sections above read as a case against the retry ladder,
159	and a future session could mistake that case for a verdict. It is not one.
160	
161	**Confirmed by measurement:**
162	
163	- *The instrument is sound.* Buffer accounting is exact — 8192.0 frames per
164	  buffer against `installTap`'s `bufferSize`, 5.859 buffers/sec against a
165	  theoretical 5.859 — and it reconciles against events it shares no code with: a
166	  605s heartbeat window was missing 14.2s of audio, and the log independently
167	  recorded a 14s outage inside it.
168	- *The aggregate really is destroyed and rebuilt per restart.* The suffix in
169	  `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>` is a per-client counter; it went `-0` →
170	  `-2` across a single unplug/replug. **Use that suffix to count churn** — it is
171	  the cheapest available measure of how many times coreaudiod has rebuilt the
172	  aggregate for us.
173	- *The ladder does run at its ceiling in the wild.* One outage produced five
174	  failed starts at 63, 63, 63 and 56 seconds apart — the once-a-minute
175	  open/close cycle, observed rather than argued.
176	- *The mic leaves on its own, often.* Two spontaneous drop-outs in ~70 minutes
177	  with nobody touching the hardware. Restart cycles are frequent even when
178	  nothing sleeps, so any per-restart cost is paid far more often than a
179	  sleep/wake-shaped mental model suggests.
180	
181	**Not confirmed, and it is the whole question:** every observed episode
182	recovered cleanly — the four-minute one, the nine-second one, and the deliberate
183	replug. Churn *happens*; it has **not** been shown to cause the wedge. The wedge
184	state (menu claiming "listening", mic dead system-wide, process alive) has not
185	recurred since the diagnostics shipped. Don't write the fix until an `AUDIO
186	STALL` line with `running=y` says which theory is right.
187	
188	> **Superseded — read the next section.** The wedge did recur, and the evidence
189	> arrived in a shape this paragraph did not anticipate: there was no `AUDIO
190	> STALL` line at all. Don't wait for one.
191	
192	**A design constraint the data did settle**, for whatever cheap availability
193	probe eventually replaces the build-an-engine-to-ask approach: a device can be
194	present in the HAL, `alive=y`, and still useless. Mid-teardown the input listed
195	as `"(unnamed)"/????/0Hz/2ch/alive=y` — readable enough to enumerate, with an
196	unreadable name, unknown transport and a **zero sample rate**. So the probe must
197	require a nonzero rate (and sane channel count), not mere presence, or it will
198	wave through starts that cannot succeed — the same trap as `outputFormat` above,
199	one layer down.
200	
201	## The wedge recurred, and it lives *below* coreaudiod (#88)
202	
203	It came back on 0.4.1, and in a third shape — **no `AUDIO STALL`, ever**. Buffers
204	were arriving at the full rate (3545 per 600s against a theoretical 3515) from a
205	device reporting `alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch`, and **every sample was exactly
206	zero**, for half an hour, system-wide — System Settings → Sound → Input showed a
207	dead meter too. Not the stall (buffers stopped), not the vanish (`inputs=NONE`):
208	the mode `AudioDiagnostics` had anticipated in a comment and never seen — a
209	device that is enumerated and streaming and *not capturing*.
210	
211	**The escalation ladder, tried in order, is the finding:**
212	
213	| Attempted | Cleared it |
214	| --- | --- |
215	| Quitting LaughCounter (full `applicationWillTerminate` teardown) | no |
216	| `sudo killall coreaudiod` | no |
217	| Physically unplugging and re-plugging the mic | **yes** |
218	
219	That settles what the release-the-mic invariant never could: **this wedge is not
220	in our process, and not in coreaudiod's user-space state either.** It survives
221	every client dying *and* the audio daemon being restarted from scratch; only a USB
222	re-enumeration takes the device out of it. Two consequences outrank the rest of
223	this file:
224	
225	- **No in-process recovery can work, so do not build one.** A restart ladder
226	  against this state is pure churn — it cannot succeed, and cycling is the thing
227	  we already believe is dangerous. The app's whole job here is to *notice fast,
228	  say so honestly, and name the one remedy that works.*
229	- **"Release the mic on every path" is necessary but not sufficient.** The
230	  teardown ran correctly on Quit and the device stayed wedged. A clean exit
231	  prevents the IOProc-abandonment cause; it does not prevent this one.
232	
233	**What shipped is reporting, not recovery.** `no signal` was already detected and
234	logged at ERROR every ten minutes — and it drove **nothing**: `isStalled` tripped
235	only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄 "listening" for the whole
236	outage while the log said the opposite. That is exactly the sin #79 set out to
237	kill, recurring one layer up, and it is why this round *again* had to be
238	reconstructed from a log instead of noticed. So `AudioDiagnostics` publishes a
239	three-state `health` (`ok` / `stalled` / `noSignal`), every user-facing surface
240	renders it, and the no-signal text says **unplug it** rather than "try Restart
241	listening" — because restarting is measured not to work. When a state has exactly
242	one remedy, the UI must name that remedy, not the generic one.
243	
244	**Detection moved off the heartbeat.** The old check ran inside the 600s heartbeat
245	block, so a dead stream was invisible for up to ten minutes and then repeated an
246	identical ERROR every ten minutes for as long as it lasted. It is judged on the 5s
247	sample tick over a 60s window of all-zero buffers now, and logged once per
248	transition. 60s is safe against a quiet room by a wide margin — a real capsule
249	always has a noise floor, and the window covers ~350 buffers.
250	
251	**"Only a replug clears it" is not "we didn't cause it."** Those are separate
252	claims and this file conflated them for one round: the ladder above establishes
253	that the state is *irreversible once triggered*, and says nothing about what
254	triggers it. The trigger question is answered below.
255	
256	## Never build an `AVAudioEngine` to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)
257	
258	This is the thing that made LaughCounter abnormal, and no other app on the owner's
259	Mac wedges the mic on sleep.
260	
261	`AudioHub.prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` → `makeEngine()`, and `makeEngine()`
262	touches `engine.inputNode`. **That property access opens the default input device
263	and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod**
264	(`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`); a failed start tears it back down. So a
265	"retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus an aggregate
266	create/destroy. One measured outage ran that cycle **~210 times over 3h40m**,
267	against hardware that was not there at all.
268	
269	Two independent things say that is the wrong shape:
270	
271	- **The information was already free.** `AudioDiagnostics` reads
272	  `kAudioHardwarePropertyDevices` and the per-device properties every five
273	  seconds, entirely with `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` property queries that open
274	  nothing. The expensive question was never buying an answer we didn't have.
275	- **The symptom shape is a known CoreAudio failure with this exact fingerprint.**
276	  `AVAudioEngine`'s hidden aggregate going stale presents as *engine running,
277	  buffers completing, no audio* — which is our no-signal state precisely, and it
278	  is documented on the output side with "only switching the device and back fixes
279	  it" (our replug). Ours had gone further than a stale aggregate, since `killall
280	  coreaudiod` did not clear it — but the failure family is the same, and we were
281	  churning the exact object at the centre of it.
282	
283	So `finishListening()` now calls `requireSettledInputDevice()` **before**
284	`prepareFormat()`, and it throws into the existing failed-start catch — so a
285	refusal reuses the whole logged/counted/retried path rather than growing a second
286	recovery mechanism beside it. Two requirements:
287	
288	- **A device the HAL says is openable**, judged by `AudioDiagnostics.hasUsableInput`:
289	  non-aggregate (counting our own aggregate would report a usable input *because*
290	  we already opened one), alive, and with a **nonzero rate and sane channel
291	  count** — mere presence is the `outputFormat` trap one layer down.
292	- **Continuously present for `deviceSettleDelay` (6s)**, which is longer than the
293	  5s sample interval, so the gate can never be satisfied by the same observation
294	  that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened the mic *in the same
295	  second it appeared* — via the config-change handler, not the ladder, which is
296	  why the gate belongs at `finishListening` where both paths meet.
297	
298	Effect on the measured outage: **~210 device opens → 0.** Nothing is opened until
299	there is something to open.
300	
301	**What is proven and what is not.** Proven: the churn was real, was
302	under-costed by its own comment, and is unlike any ordinary audio app. *Not*
303	proven: that it caused the wedge. The mic reported a sane `48000Hz/2ch/alive=y`
304	when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the mid-enumeration story
305	specifically. Treat this as removing the only mechanism by which we could
306	plausibly damage a device — not as a confirmed root-cause fix. **If it recurs,
307	that is information, not a reason to assume the gate failed.**
308	
309	### A settle gate applies to arrivals you *witnessed*, not to what was already there
310	
311	The gate above shipped in 0.5.0 with a bug that made the app look broken on every
312	launch: it refused to start listening for ~19 seconds, which reads as "it doesn't
313	start" and sent the owner to the menu to switch it on by hand.
314	
315	Two things compounded:
316	
317	- **`Timer(timeInterval:repeats:)` does not fire immediately.** The first sample
318	  lands one `sampleInterval` (5s) *after* `AudioDiagnostics.start()`, and
319	  `usableInputSince` was only ever set inside `sample()` — so for the app's first
320	  five seconds the probe reported "no input device" about a microphone sitting
321	  right there. Any state a timer maintains needs **seeding at start**, not just
322	  updating on tick.
323	- **Then the settle clock started from first observation**, costing another 6s,
324	  and the retry ladder's 2→4→8s backoff pushed the first viable attempt to ~19s.
325	
326	The conceptual error is the second one, and it is the reusable lesson: *"it
327	appeared N seconds ago" is a claim you can only make about a transition you
328	watched happen.* A device that was already present when sampling began has been
329	there for as long as the Mac has been up; there is no enumeration race to lose,
330	and waiting is pure cost. So `usableInputFor` reports `.greatestFiniteMagnitude`
331	for a device found already present (`witnessedArrival == false`), and a real
332	duration only for one seen to arrive — which is exactly the wedge case the gate
333	exists for, and still gets its full settle window.
334	
335	### A continuity claim cannot span a gap in observation — and sleep is one (#107)
336	
337	The wedge recurred on 0.5.0, after a sleep, **with the settle gate in place and
338	doing nothing**: menu bar on ⚠️ *no signal*, and System Settings → Sound → Input
339	showing a dead meter, the same system-wide shape as #88.
340	
341	The gate was a no-op on the wake path, in both 0.5.0 and the 0.5.1 refinement
342	above, for one reason: `usableInputSince` was carried straight *through* the
343	sleep. `AudioDiagnostics`' sampling timer does not fire while the machine is
344	asleep, so a mic that powered down, re-enumerated and came back was still
345	reported as having been continuously present since before the sleep — in 0.5.0 as
346	a long elapsed run, in 0.5.1 as `.greatestFiniteMagnitude` via
347	`witnessedArrival == false`. Either way `requireSettledInputDevice()` passed
348	instantly and the resume opened the device with **zero** settle: precisely the
349	"opened it in the same second it appeared" hazard the gate was added to stop, on
350	precisely the transition it was built for.
351	
352	The reusable shape, and the one to check against any future "it has been X for N
353	seconds" state: **a duration is a claim about a span you observed, so it is only
354	as good as the observation behind it.** The previous section established that
355	"already present when we started watching" needs no settle window; the missing
356	half is that the clause only holds *while you are still watching*. A blind spot
357	inside the run invalidates the whole run, because what the run asserts —
358	"nothing happened to this device" — is exactly what a blind spot cannot support.
359	
360	So `AudioDiagnostics` tracks observation as its own state:
361	
362	- **`inputAvailability` is a three-state enum, not a duration-or-nil.**
363	  `.absent` ("no default input device worth opening") and `.unobserved` ("we have
364	  not been watching") are different answers and only one of them is about the
365	  hardware. Collapsing them would have put an unmeasured claim about the mic into
366	  the log — the sin #79 and #88 were both about.
367	- **`noteObservationInterrupted()` is called from `willSleep`**, so a sleep is
368	  *declared* rather than inferred. Inferring it from elapsed time misses a sleep
369	  shorter than the tolerance, and the USB bus is powered down for a short sleep
370	  too. The elapsed-time backstop in `sample()` stays for interruptions nobody
371	  announces — and it must measure with **`Date()`, not `systemUptime`**, the one
372	  place in this file that inverts the usual rule: the span being measured is the
373	  span the monotonic clock refuses to count.
374	- **The run is keyed on the device's UID**, not on "is anything usable?". A mic
375	  swapped for another between two samples is a new arrival that has settled for
376	  zero seconds, and a set-level predicate cannot see that happen at all.
377	- **`usableInput()` judges the *system default* input**, which is the device
378	  `AVAudioEngine` actually opens — a healthy mic behind a broken default is not a
379	  mic we can capture from. That also subsumes the old exclude-aggregates rule
380	  (our hidden `CADefaultDeviceAggregate` is never the system default) and fixes
381	  its collateral damage: a user's deliberately-built aggregate device is a fine
382	  thing to capture from, and the old predicate refused it.
383	
384	**Still unproven, and still the whole question:** that opening a device
385	mid-enumeration is what wedges it. This recurrence is *consistent* with the
386	theory — the gate meant to prevent it was inert across sleep, which is when the
387	wedge keeps happening — but consistency is not proof, and the same recurrence is
388	equally consistent with the gate being irrelevant. What it does settle is
389	narrower and worth keeping separate: **the mitigation shipped in 0.5.0 was never
390	actually exercised on the wake path**, so 0.5.0 recurring says nothing about
391	whether the mitigation works. The next recurrence is the first one that will.
392	
393	## Diagnostics must not assume a toolchain on the owner's Mac
394	
395	The Mac running LaughCounter installs the DMG from CI and has **no Xcode command
396	line tools** — so anything needed to diagnose a live failure has to be either
397	shell built into macOS, or compiled into the app by CI. That is why the HAL reads
398	live in the app rather than in a helper script.
399	
400	`command -v swift` does **not** test for a Swift toolchain: `/usr/bin/swift`
401	ships on every Mac as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer
402	tools?"* dialog when run, so the check passes and the script prompts the owner to
403	install 8 GB of Xcode. Gate on `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1` first — it fails
404	quietly when the tools are absent.
405	
406	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself
407	
408	`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
409	`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
410	a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
411	terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
412	those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
413	SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal
414	default. SIGKILL/Force-Quit/crash remain uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug.
415	Don't add `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` to Info.plist: it would let logout
416	SIGKILL the app past all of this.
417	
418	## Deferred work must be generation-guarded
419	
420	`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
421	delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
422	stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or
423	un-settled at wake. Every intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every
424	delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.
425	When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /
426	`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
427	all future starts.
428	
429	## There is no "returned from standby" notification — fan in, then coalesce
430	
431	macOS distinguishes sleep depths internally but exposes no standby-specific event:
432	`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
433	machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
434	re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
435	`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
436	`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires
437	several of them in a burst and each must not schedule its own restart:
438	
439	- **Coalesce with an id, not a bool.** `pendingResumeID` holds the one in-flight
440	  resume; a stale timer compares its captured id and returns without touching
441	  state. A bare `resumePending` bool deadlocks: a re-sleep during the delay
442	  invalidates the timer, the timer clears the bool, and whichever of the two
443	  orderings loses leaves the next wake either unable to schedule (flag stuck true)
444	  or double-scheduling.
445	- **Gate on owing a resume**, i.e. `sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`.
446	  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
447	  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
448	- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
449	  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
450	- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
451	  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
452	  three workspace triggers still cover the case.
453	
454	## Resume by *intent*, and retry — a failed post-standby start has no second event
455	
456	`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
457	`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
458	without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
459	active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
460	Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.
461	
462	The intent is stored as `offReason: String?` — nil means "meant to be running" and
463	`listeningIntent` is derived from it — rather than a bool beside a separate reason
464	string. The menu status, the tooltip and the wake log all render that one field, so
465	they cannot disagree about whether the counter is off or why ("paused",
466	"no microphone access", "starting up"). Menu **Pause listening** sets it; every
467	request to listen clears it, which is what asking to listen means.
468	
469	After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
470	re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
471	config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
472	sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
473	`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every
474	success / system return / manual resume. Bounded on purpose (a mic that is gone for
475	good emits nothing and must not be polled forever) and slow on purpose (rapid-cycling
476	is what wedges the mic). The wake settle is also stretched 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep
477	lasted longer than `standbyThreshold`; measure that span with `Date()`, **not**
478	`ProcessInfo.systemUptime`, which does not advance while the machine is asleep.
479	
480	## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop
481	
482	CoreAudio posts `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` for our *own* stop/start
483	(react → infinite restart loop, hence the suppress window) **and** for genuine
484	device events — including while the machine heads into sleep (hence the
485	`sleeping` gate from `willSleep` until the post-wake settle). A genuine event
486	swallowed by the window is reconciled at settle time by *state*, not by the
487	notification: engine dead while `listening` → restart; start failed and an
488	event arrived → one retry per swallowed event (a dead mic emits no events, so
489	this can't poll).
490	
491	## Misc gotchas that bit
492	
493	- `engine.stop()` unconditionally in `AudioHub.stop()`: it's safe when not
494	  running and it releases what `prepare()` allocated — a prepare-then-throw
495	  path would otherwise keep the input unit holding the device.
496	- `installTap` with a format the hardware no longer matches raises an
497	  **uncatchable NSException** — re-validate the live format immediately before
498	  the tap (narrows, doesn't eliminate; there is no atomic API).
499	- `SFSpeechRecognizer` fed via `SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest` never
500	  holds the device — it can't cause the wedge. But its state is touched from
501	  main, the Speech callback queue, *and* the audio tap thread: everything in
502	  `VoiceCommand` goes through one lock, and the two-phase `start()` gates the
503	  task store on *request identity* (`request === newRequest`), because a
504	  restart() between the phases leaves `running == true` — gating on `running`
505	  would store a dead task and permanently block the idempotency guard.

# The microphone's lifecycle — an app that must never damage the device it uses

LaughCounter holds a real microphone open for hours at a time, and the hardware
answers back: a USB webcam mic can be left **wedged** — dead system-wide, no
input meter anywhere, until it is physically re-plugged. Every rule here exists
because that happened, repeatedly, on the owner's Mac.

The checks in this pack hold the three mechanical parts (only `AudioHub` builds
an engine; termination signals reach `applicationWillTerminate`; the app never
opts into sudden termination). What follows is the judgment half — the rules a
scan cannot decide. The **case history** — which release, which measurement,
which theory survived — lives in
[`dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md`](../../../../dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md)
and stays there; don't copy it here, read it before touching engine start/stop,
sleep/wake, exit handling, or `VoiceCommand`.

**Never open the device to ask a question about it.** `AudioHub.makeEngine()`
touches `engine.inputNode`, and that property access opens the default input and
mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod
(`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`) — so a "cheap format read" in a retry
ladder is really a device open plus an aggregate create/destroy, measured at ~210
of them over 3h40m against hardware that was not there. Availability questions go
to `AudioDiagnostics`, which answers from `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` property
queries that open nothing. Cycling the device is the one mechanism by which this
app could plausibly damage it, so the cost of an answer is a property of the API
you ask, not of how often you ask.

**Presence is not usability, at any layer.** `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` reports a
plausible 48 kHz with the input torn down while `inputFormat` reports 0, so a
guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that cannot succeed
(`AudioHub.validatedFormat()` requires both, and requires them to agree). One
layer down, a device can be enumerated and `alive=y` with a zero sample rate and
an unreadable name mid-teardown — so `AudioDiagnostics.hasUsableInput` demands a
nonzero rate and a sane channel count, not mere presence. Any new probe inherits
this: whatever it reads, ask what that field says while the mic is absent.

**A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N
seconds" is only as good as the watching behind it, and the sampling timer does
not fire while the Mac sleeps — which is why the settle gate was inert on exactly
the wake path it was built for (#107). Hence `inputAvailability` distinguishes
`.absent` from `.unobserved`, `noteObservationInterrupted()` is called from
`willSleep` so a sleep is declared rather than inferred, and the run is keyed on
the device's UID so a swap counts as a new arrival. Any future "X has been true
for N seconds" state gets the same three questions: was I watching, is it the
same device, and what does a gap in observation do to the claim?

**Pick the clock by whether the span may contain a sleep.** `systemUptime` for
"how long has the stream been silent *while we were awake*" (buffer accounting,
stall windows); `Date()` for anything that can span a sleep — the sleep-duration
stamp in `AppDelegate` and the elapsed-time interruption backstop in
`AudioDiagnostics`. Both directions are wrong the other way round, and each site
in the sources says which it is and why.

**Deferred work must be generation-guarded.** `asyncAfter` timers scheduled
before a sleep fire *immediately* on wake, so a delayed start that a stop raced
with would re-acquire the mic going into sleep or un-settled at wake. Every
intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every delayed closure captures it and
aborts if it moved. When cancelling in-flight restarts, reset
`restartInFlight` / `restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange` too, or the latches
stay stuck and block all future starts. Coalesce the wake fan-in with an **id**,
not a bool — a bool deadlocks when a re-sleep lands during the delay.

**Never claim to be listening on the strength of `engine.start()` returning.**
That is what let the menu bar say 😄 *listening* through an entire evening of a
dead device, and it is why both wedge investigations had to be reconstructed from
logs instead of noticed. State shown to the user is derived from
`AudioDiagnostics.health` (`ok` / `stalled` / `noSignal`) — measured buffers —
and when a state has exactly one known remedy the UI names *that* remedy
(no-signal says unplug the mic; "Restart listening" is measured not to work).

**Compile-green is not a gate for this code.** CI runs `swift build` and nothing
else, and every raise-vs-throw bug in this area is invisible to the compiler and
reachable in the first second of a run — two crash-on-launch builds shipped past
it. A change to `AudioHub`, the restart machinery, or the sleep/wake path is not
verified until it has actually started on a Mac. Reproduce the interesting case
without waiting for hardware to misbehave: let the display sleep, and coreaudiod
tears its contexts down seconds later.

**Assume no toolchain on the machine that runs it.** The owner's Mac installs the
DMG from CI and has no Xcode command line tools, so anything needed to diagnose a
live failure is either shell built into macOS or compiled into the app by CI —
that is why the HAL reads live in `AudioDiagnostics` rather than in a helper
script. `command -v swift` does **not** test for a toolchain (`/usr/bin/swift` is
a stub that prompts for an 8 GB install); gate on `xcode-select -p` instead.

{"number":121,"title":"Claudinite growth: discover local pack macos-audio-lifecycle","body":"Weekly `growth-discover-packs` run. Refs #112.

## The gap

Manifesting the repo's stack turned up one technology domain with a large body of real, hard-won knowledge and no pack homing it: **the macOS microphone lifecycle** — `AVAudioEngine`, CoreAudio device state, and the sleep/wake and exit paths around them.

- **No canon pack homes it.** The shelf is `basics`, `barriers`, `git-github`, `github-actions`, `grow_with_claudinite`, `tidy-repo`.
- **Neither local pack owns it.** `local/on-device-privacy` owns the privacy boundary; `local/laughcounter` owns the repo's general build/packaging and check-authoring lessons.
- **The knowledge is real and unenforced.** `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` is 505 lines of case history across #22 / #61 / #72 / #76 / #79 / #88 / #107, and nothing mechanically held any of it.

## What lands

`.claudinite/local/packs/macos-audio-lifecycle/`, declared as `local/macos-audio-lifecycle`.

Three checks, each red on a fixture and green on the repo's real files (`node --test .claudinite/local/packs/macos-audio-lifecycle/pack.test.mjs`, 9 tests):

| Check | Rule | Grounded in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `engine-construction-confined` | only `AudioHub` builds an `AVAudioEngine` | `AudioHub.makeEngine()` materializes `inputNode`, which opens the default input and mints a hidden coreaudiod aggregate — one outage ran that ~210 times in 3h40m (#88); `AudioDiagnostics` exists so nothing else has to |
| `signal-teardown-routing` | a tree that installs an audio tap must route SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP to `NSApp.terminate`, with `SIG_IGN` before `resume()` | `main.swift`; NSApplication installs no signal handlers, so a bare SIGTERM abandons the tap's IOProc (#22) |
| `no-sudden-termination` | `mac/Resources/*.plist` never declares `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` | it would let logout SIGKILL the app past every teardown path |

The judgment half lands as `RULES.md` prose: open no device to ask a question about it; presence is not usability at any layer; a duration is only as good as the observation behind it (#107); clock choice across sleep; generation-guarded deferred work; never claim "listening" on `engine.start()` returning (#79); compile-green is not a gate for this code; assume no toolchain on the owner's Mac.

The **case history stays in `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md`** rather than being copied into the pack — `RULES.md` carries the invariants and points at it, so there is one source for the narrative.

Also narrows `local/laughcounter`'s `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` so the new territory routes cleanly out of the catch-all pack.

## Review notes

`check_the_world` and `check_the_work` are clean with the pack declared. **Auto-merge is deliberately not armed** — a new pack's checks reach every session and every CI run the moment this merges, so a human reviews it. The one check with a knowable false-positive shape is `signal-teardown-routing`'s ordering arm, which compares first-occurrence offsets rather than parsing scopes; the tradeoff is written into the file's header comment.
